item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=How+do+systematic+classification+and+dehumanization+processes+in+multi-agent+environments+interfere+with+independent+ethical+judgment+and+obedience+limits%3F&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.5220/0010240500690079\", \"title\": [\"A Systematic Review about Requirements Engineering Processes for Multi-Agent Systems\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.5220/0010240500690079\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2021]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6315059\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence in Military Decision-Making Operational Effectiveness, Human Judgment, and Ethical Limits\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence into modern military operations has transformed how information is processed, and decisions are made in combat environments. This paper examines the extent of how AI-assisted decision-making improves operational effectiveness without undermining human command and ethical responsibility. Focusing on United States military applications of AI in intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and defensive systems, the analysis evaluates both performance gains (speed, consistency, and data fusion) and risks. Applying an ethical framework grounded in human-in-the-loop principles and Just War Theory, this paper identifies key failure modes such as automation bias. The findings argue that while AI systems can meaningfully enhance tactical effectiveness, their unbounded use risks weakening the human judgment necessary for lawful and morally accountable military action. The paper concludes that AI should be treated as a force multiplier rather than an autonomous decision authority, and that its legitimacy in military operations depends on clearly defined constraints that preserve meaningful human control over lethal decision making.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6315059\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7328440\", \"title\": [\"Between Decision and Dialogue: Ethical Limits and Practical Judgment in Labor Arbitration\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This essay examines when, if ever, a U.S. labor arbitrator may ethically encourage parties to pursue a negotiated resolution rather than proceed …
